newsitem.title: ITALY: Executed O'Dell buried in adopted city Palermo.
newsitem.headline: Executed O'Dell buried in adopted city Palermo.

text.p: The body of convicted rapist and murderer Joseph O'Dell was buried on Thursday in Palermo, the city which led a vocal but ultimately futile campaign to save him from execution in the United States.
While hundreds turned out for the ceremony, others remained puzzled by Italy's fascination with O'Dell's case and one senator branded the burial a "farce."
O'Dell, who was killed by lethal injection in the state of Virginia last week, was entombed in Palermo's Santa Maria di Gesu cemetery after an emotional Catholic church service.

Around 400 mourners, most of them ordinary Sicilians, crammed into the tiny stuccoed chapel to hear the service, which was also broadcast to more than 100 people sheltering under the shade of pine trees in the picturesque courtyard outside.
O'Dell's widow Lori Urs was there, along with his spiritual advisor Sister Helen Prejean and Palermo's mayor Leoluca Orlando, who flew to the U.S. last week in a failed 11th hour bid to save O'Dell.
Urs, who married O'Dell just hours before his death, told reporters after the funeral that she thought her husband's execution was a shameful episode in U.S. history.

"I discovered suppressed evidence, prosecution misconduct, unethical behaviour, witness tampering, and a sort of an effort to kill a man based upon such lies that I had to wonder why," she told a news conference.
"Sadly, as a I searched for answers...I was told "this is the way it is".
Many Italians took O'Dell's case to their heart, not necessarily because they thought he was innocent, but rather as an expression of their opposition to the death penalty.
"It is not for us to say if you were guilty, and we do not want to make a hero out of you," priest Pierto Sorci said in an address to the funeral, speaking over O'Dell's walnut coffin.
"Joseph, you were a sinner, just like those who killed you, who appealed to a law which was written by other sinners.
"Thank you for choosing this city as your place of rest," Sorci said.
Palermo, perhaps more than any other city in the world, championed the cause of O'Dell, who was executed for the 1985 rape and murder of Helen Schartner.
The city made him an honorary citizen and O'Dell responded by asking for his body to be buried here.
"Joseph O'Dell III" his tombstone read. "Honorary Citizen of Palermo, Killed by Virginia, U.S.A. in the name of a merciless and brutal justice system. September 20 1941 - July 23 1997."
Sister Prejean, author of the book "Dead Man Walking" and an ardent campaigner for the abolition of the death penalty, recalled the night of July 23 when O'Dell died.

"Never have I seen a person face death so calm, so self-posessed, so loving," she told a news conference. "When the state of Virginia killed him, he was the freeest man, the most loving man in the room."

"I believe history is being made today. The body of a death row inmate executed in the U.S. has been claimed by the people of Italy and carried across the ocean to be buried with love and reverence in Palermo."
But not everyone was happy with the decision to honour a man who had a long criminal record and no known ties with Italy.
"It's a grotesque farce," senator Valentino Martelli of the rightist National Alliance party told parliament on Wednesday.
